questions.q: Does custom Apex REST get an automatic versioning mechanism the way Salesforce's standard REST API does?
options: Only for SOAP web services, not REST
Yes, every Apex REST class is automatically versioned by API version
No — versioning a custom Apex REST service is a deliberate design decision the developer has to make
Only if the class is marked global
questions.explain: The standard REST API bakes a version number into its URL automatically; a custom Apex REST service gets no equivalent built-in mechanism and must be versioned by design.

questions.q: In the URL-path versioning pattern, how are v1 and v2 of a service typically separated?
options: By using the same class and the same urlMapping for both
By changing the org's API version setting
By using two different Named Credentials
By mapping them to different urlMapping values, such as /v1/Accounts/* and /v2/Accounts/*, usually as separate classes
questions.explain: Because each HTTP-verb annotation can only be used once per class, a breaking change typically means a new class with a new urlMapping, isolating the old and new versions.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off of the in-payload versioning pattern (one URL, a version field in the request body)?
options: It avoids proliferating URLs and classes, but couples all versions' logic together in one class, risking the old version's code when adding new logic
It cannot be used with JSON payloads
It automatically generates a WSDL for each version
It requires a separate Connected App for each version
questions.explain: In-payload versioning keeps one URL but mixes all version branches into a single class, unlike URL-path versioning which keeps them fully isolated.

questions.q: Why is silently changing an existing published version's response shape especially risky for an inbound Apex REST service?
options: Because it is not risky — Salesforce automatically migrates external callers
Because external callers live outside the org entirely, so the change can break them with no warning and without being caught by the org's own test suite
Because it would violate the 100-callouts-per-transaction limit
Because Apex REST classes cannot be redeployed once published
questions.explain: External callers' code isn't part of the Salesforce org's own deploy and test process, so a silent breaking change can surface only when their integration fails in production.

questions.q: When should a version strategy for a custom inbound web service ideally be planned?
options: Only once the service exceeds 100 callouts per transaction
Only after the first external caller reports a breaking change
Before the first external caller ever integrates against the service
Version strategy is unnecessary for inbound services
questions.explain: Planning a version strategy up front is far cheaper than retrofitting one after external systems have already built against an unversioned contract.
